title: The Faden Procedure: Masterclass in Posterior Fixation
summary: The Faden operation, or Cüppers' posterior fixation suture, is a sophisticated strabismus technique designed to selectively weaken a rectus muscle in its field of action without significantly altering its primary position function. It is the gold standard for managing dynamic, incomitant deviations and dissociated vertical deviation (DVD).

sections.title: Definition & Physiological Concept
sections.content: Introduced by Cüppers in 1974, the Faden (German for 'thread') procedure involves anchoring the belly of a rectus muscle to the sclera significantly posterior to its anatomical insertion. This creates a 'new' functional insertion, effectively shortening the active lever arm and reducing the torque exerted by the muscle as the eye rotates into its field of action. Crucially, because the original insertion remains intact, the muscle's pull in the primary position is largely unchanged.

sections.title: Essential Instrumentation & Materials
content: Suture: 5-0 or 6-0 non-absorbable (Mersilene or Prolene) is mandatory to prevent late failure.
Needle: Spatulated 1/2 or 3/8 circle needle to minimize scleral perforation risk.
Retraction: Long Desmarres or Schepens retractors for deep orbital exposure.
Callipers: Castroviejo or specialized curved calipers for retroequatorial measurement.
Fixation: Headlight is essential for visualizing the posterior sclera.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Surgical Technique
content: 1. Conjunctival Incision: Limbal or fornix approach; wide exposure required.
2. Muscle Isolation: Secure the muscle with a 6-0 Vicryl suture (if combined with recession) or a muscle hook.
3. Posterior Exposure: Use long retractors to expose the sclera 12-16mm behind the insertion. Beware of the Vortex veins.
4. Scleral Marking: Use calipers to mark the exact posterior distance on both sides of the muscle belly.
5. Scleral Pass: Perform two partial-thickness scleral bites at the marked sites. Ensure the pass is deep enough for stability but avoids perforation.
6. Muscle Inclusion: Pass the suture through the outer 1/3 of the muscle belly on each side.
7. Tying: Secure the knots tightly, effectively pinning the muscle to the sclera at the new posterior point.
8. Closure: Standard conjunctival closure with 8-0 Vicryl.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: When to Faden vs. Recess
Red Flags & Intraoperative Warnings
content: Vortex Vein Injury: Specifically when operating on the SR (superior-temporal) or IR (inferior-nasal/temporal).
Scleral Perforation: The sclera is significantly thinner posterior to the equator (0.3mm).
Optic Nerve Proximity: Extreme posterior passes on the MR can approach the optic nerve.
Inferior Rectus Faden: High risk of affecting lower lid height (retraction) and Sympathetic supply.
Inadequate Suture Depth: Non-absorbable sutures 'cheesewiring' through the muscle belly.

content.explanation: To remember distances behind insertion: Medial (12mm), Superior (13-14mm), Lateral (15mm). 'M-S-L' sounds like 'Muscle'.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Postoperative Adhesions: Can lead to restricted motility beyond the intended effect.
Slipped Muscle: If the suture fails or bites are too superficial.
Chronic Pain/Foreign Body Sensation: Due to the use of non-absorbable bulky sutures.
Endophthalmitis: Secondary to unrecognized scleral perforation.
Prognosis: Excellent for High AC/A ratio ET and DVD; less predictable in paralytic cases.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls: The Expert's Edge
content: Always perform the Faden on the fixating eye to maximize the effect on the fellow eye via Hering's Law.
For DVD, combining a Superior Rectus recession (7-9mm) with a Faden at 14mm is more effective than recession alone.
Avoid the IR Faden if possible; it is technically the most difficult and prone to complications.
Ensure the suture is tied *before* the muscle is recessed (if doing both) to ensure accurate placement.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent literature highlights the 'Adjustable Faden' technique using a sliding knot system to fine-tune the posterior fixation post-operatively. Landmark studies by von Noorden and others have confirmed that while Faden is highly effective for nystagmus blockage, it should be reserved for cases where the 'null point' is achieved via convergence. Modern imaging (MRI) has shown that the Faden procedure significantly alters the 'muscle path' and pulley interactions, adding a mechanical component to its physiological effect.
